deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. Olbers found Vesta on 29 March 1807. The surrounding pages hold Vesta observations and solar places for March 29 to April 22, 1807. On this page Gauss (a) computes the Sun's place for April 10, 14 and 18 (9h mean time, Bremen) and (b) fits an elliptic orbit to Vesta from two heliocentric places, 29 March and 14 April. He uses exactly the machinery later printed in Theoria Motus (1809), Book I, Sect. 3, arts. 88 ff.

A. SOLAR PLACES (three parallel blocks).

Table sum. Each block adds the epoch line (8°16'27.10; 7462.90; 769, 658, 684, 297) to the motion for n days.
- Columns: mean longitude L0; mean anomaly counted from apogee in units of 1/10000 of a circle; perturbation arguments in 1/1000 of a circle (probably Moon, Venus, Mars, Jupiter; the last, 297..., probably the nutation/node argument; my interpretation).
- April 10 (n=10): 18°7'50.40, 7736.68, 108, 675, 709, 298.
- April 14 (n=14): 22°4'23.72, 7846.19, 243, 682, 719, 299.
- April 18 (n=18): 26°0'57.04, 7955.70, 379, 689, 729, 300.
- The daily motions are 0.9856472° and 27.38 units per day, i.e. the solar mean motion. So 7736.68 units = 278.5° = mean anomaly + 180°.

True longitude. Gauss adds the equation of centre (+1°53'48.74, +1°52'12.62, +1°50'5.30) and a −1.36 / −1.36 / −1.33 table correction. He then adds four small terms. The first three are planetary perturbations (+4.71 −10.37 +8.15 for April 10). The last, about +37.1–37.2, is nearly constant over all dates; it is presumably a combined nutation/aberration/table-constant correction (my guess). Results:
- April 10: λ = 20°2'17.44.
- April 14: λ = 23°57'17.35.
- April 18: λ = 27°51'40.97.

Radius vector. Tabular value plus three perturbation terms:
- April 10: R = 1.0027625+286−54+33 = 1.0027890, log R = 0.0012096.
- April 14: R = 1.0038901, log R = 0.0016861.
- April 18: R = 1.0049709, log R = 0.0021535.

Obliquity. Apparent ε = 23°27'52.86 − 2.95 (nutation) = 23°27'49.91.

Equatorial coordinates of the Sun. The log columns are: log cos λ; log(R cos ε); log sin λ; log(R sin ε). For April 10 these are 9.9728804, 9.9637263, 9.5348460, 9.6012792. From them:
- X = R cos λ
- Y = R sin λ cos ε
- Z = R sin λ sin ε
Results:
- April 10: (0.9420844, 0.3151899, 0.1368123).
- April 14: (0.9174208, 0.3738920, 0.1622927).
- April 18: (0.8884753, 0.4308217, 0.1870038).

B. ORBIT FROM TWO RADII (left and centre).

Input. log r = 0.3637999 and log r' = 0.3625042, difference 0.0012957. Gauss's half-angle symbols are used throughout: f = ½(v'−v), F = ½(v+v'), g = ½(E'−E), G = ½(E+E').
- f = 2°14'23.435, so ½f = 1°7'11.7175.
- log √(rr') = 0.36315205.

Auxiliary angle ω. tan(45°+ω) = (r'/r)^(1/4), with ¼Δlog = 0.00032394. This gives ω = 1'16.9125″ and 2ω = 2'33.825″.

Gauss's l.
- log sin ½f = 8.2910373.
- log sin²½f = 6.5820746.
- log tan 2ω = 6.8725737, so log tan²2ω = 3.7451474.
- log cos f = 9.9996681.
- l = sin²½f/cos f + tan²2ω/cos f = 0.00038230193 + 0.00000055652 = 0.00038285845.
- Also written: 5/6 = 0.8333333, the constant of the y-equation, h = m²/(5/6 + l + ξ).

Gauss's x. With ½g = 1°7'43.0693:
- x = sin²½g = 0.00038797351.
- l + x = 0.00077083196, which is m²/y² in Gauss's notation.
- Also written: ½f+½g = 2°14'54.7868 and ½f−½g = −31.3518″.

Anomalies.
- ½(F+G) = 101°31'14.131 and ½(F−G) = 1°5'16.907.
- Hence F = 102°36'31.038 and G = 100°25'57.224.
- v = F−f = 100°22'7.603 and v' = F+f = 104°50'54.473.
- g = 2°15'26.139, so E = G−g = 98°10'31.085 and E' = G+g = 102°41'23.363.

Eccentricity. log e = 8.5885323 (e = 0.038774). Then log e″ = 8.5885323 − 4.6855749 = 3.9029574, i.e. e″ = 7997.7″.

Mean anomalies (Kepler's equation).
- log sin E = 9.9955640, giving e″ sin E = 2°11'56.2855.
- log sin E' = 9.9892600, giving e″ sin E' = 2°10'2.2055.
- M = E − e sin E = 95°58'34.7995 (March 29).
- M' = 100°31'21.1575 (April 14).

Mean motion.
- log a = 0.3601163, so log a^(3/2) = 0.54017445.
- log k″ = 3.5500066 (k = 3548.1876″ per day).
- Hence n = 1022.8975″ per day, i.e. 1°8'11.5895 per 4 days.
- Tabulated M at 4-day steps: 95°58'34.80, 97°6'46.39, 98°14'57.98, 99°23'9.57, 100°31'21.16 (continued on the next page).
- log b = log a + log√(1−e²) = 0.3601163 + 9.9996733 = 0.3597896.

Elements and equatorial constants.
- Node 108°31'17.05, inclination 7°23'21.82; 'Perih. 82°47'37.97' and '−25°43'39.08' are also written, meaning not determined.
- Constants A, B, C = 172°56'17.82, 85°37'59.26, 65°24'13.17, revised to 172°55'58.88, 85°38'11.04, 65°25'11.89.
- Log amplitudes 0.3565409, 0.3304409, 9.9371163, and additive constants −0.0108413, −0.0827394, −0.0305065. These are presumably −ae times the direction cosines.
- They serve the eccentric-anomaly form x = α sin(A+E) + const, used on the next page.
- The two columns 0.3568627/0.3565360 etc. differ by exactly 0.0003267 = −log√(1−e²), i.e. they are the a- and b-versions.

Unexplained trial figures: several scratch lines (0.3006981, 6.5888020, 8.5919843 'inf', 8.59366–8.59383, 6.1818374n, the interpolations 1.6.39 849/1086, and the top-margin additions) look like trial iterations or checks. I cannot reconstruct them with certainty.
errors: No substantive errors found; every addition and subtraction I re-did (table sums, equation-of-centre steps, radius-vector corrections, F±G, E = G∓g, M = E − e sin E, the 4-day mean-motion progression) checks to the last digit.
Minor: log tan 2ω is written 6.8725737; direct conversion of 153.825″ gives about 6.872603. This is a ~3e-5 discrepancy, under 0.01″ in 2ω, and of no consequence for l.
Minor: ω from ¼Δlog r = 0.000323925 gives about 76.92″ versus Gauss's 76.9125″, an insignificant difference.
The perturbation/constant terms (+37.1″ etc.) and the 'inf 8.5919843' line cannot be fully verified from this page alone.

results.what: Computation of the Sun's longitude, radius vector and geocentric equatorial rectangular coordinates from von Zach-type solar tables (argument sums, equation of centre, perturbations, nutation, obliquity).
results.modern_name: Solar ephemeris reduction / solar rectangular coordinates
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th-c. practice (tables by von Zach, Delambre)

results.what: Orbit from two heliocentric radii and the included angle via Gauss's auxiliary angle ω (tan(45°+ω) = (r'/r)^(1/4)), l = (sin²½f + tan²2ω)/cos f, x = sin²½g, the 5/6 term of the y-equation, and eccentric anomalies from F, G, f, g.
results.modern_name: Gauss's method for the ratio of sector to triangle (two-position / Lambert problem)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Theoria Motus (1809), Book I, Sect. 3, arts. 88-97

results.what: Mean anomalies via Kepler's equation (M = E − e″ sin E) and the mean motion n = k/a^(3/2) with Gauss's constant (log k″ = 3.5500066), tabulated at 4-day intervals.
Equatorial 'Gaussian constants' (A, B, C and log amplitudes, additive −ae terms) for computing heliocentric equatorial coordinates of Vesta directly from the eccentric anomaly.
results.modern_name: Gaussian vectorial / equatorial constants (P, Q form)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working draft of Gauss's well-known April 1807 computation of Vesta's first orbit. It uses methods published in Theoria Motus two years later, and the Vesta computation itself is historically documented. Its value is as a dated pre-publication instance of the sector–triangle machinery (ω, l, x, 5/6), not as a new result.

transcription_corrections: '9.9992600' should be 9.9892600 (log sin ε', as on the next page's list).
'9.2910373' (left column) is log sin ½f = 8.2910373; its double gives 6.5820746.
Labels '½F+G', '½F−G' mean ½(F+G), ½(F−G); likewise '½f+g', '½f−g', which are ½f ± ½g.
In the April 10 table line the struck digits are overwritten; the values consistent with the sums are 25 (Mars column, 684+25 = 709) and 1 (last column, 297+1 = 298).
'1,0038907' (April 14) is corrected in the manuscript; with the listed corrections it gives 1,0038901.
